```{r knitr-options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = FALSE, comment = "#>",
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center",
                      dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 92)
```

When students learn together, regulation is a shared activity. Members of a
group plan the task, monitor their progress, discuss and reach consensus,
adapt when something fails and attend to the emotional climate of the group.
These moves are not independent: a plan invites a response, a disagreement
calls for discussion, and a moment of cohesion often precedes a decision.
The temporal order of regulatory moves is therefore as informative as their
frequency, and transition network analysis (Saqr et al., 2025) has made the
first-order transitions between them a standard object of study in learning
analytics.

A first-order transition model assumes that the next move depends on the
current move alone. Whether that assumption holds is an empirical question.
A variable-order transition tree, the prediction suffix tree of Ron, Singer
and Tishby (1996), lets each history keep as much of its past as the data
support: a context such as `consensus -> cohesion` gets its own next-move
distribution only when it predicts differently from the shorter context
`cohesion`. The same idea underlies variable-length Markov chains (Bühlmann
& Wyner, 1999).

This case study addresses three questions about collaborative regulation.
First, how do regulatory moves follow one another? Second, how much history
is needed to predict the next move, and which longer pathways reproducibly
change the prediction? Third, do high and low achievers move through
regulation differently, and does that difference survive when the course in
which they studied is held fixed?

```{r setup}
library(transitiontrees)
```

## Data

`group_regulation_long` is a bundled event log of coded collaborative
regulation, one row per regulatory move. The variables play the following
roles:

- **Actor:** `Actor` — the student; each student contributes one sequence of
  moves.
- **Time:** `Time` — the timestamp of each move; it orders the moves and,
  through the default 15-minute gap rule, would split a student's moves into
  separate sessions.
- **State:** `Action` — the regulatory move, one of nine codes (`adapt`,
  `cohesion`, `consensus`, `coregulate`, `discuss`, `emotion`, `monitor`,
  `plan`, `synthesis`).
- **Grouping:** `Achiever` — the student's achievement level, `High` or `Low`.
- **Context:** `Group` — the collaboration group, and `Course` — the course,
  `A`, `B` or `C`.

The design matters for the group comparison, so the distribution of moves
over courses and achievement levels comes first.

```{r design}
with(group_regulation_long, table(Course, Achiever))
```

Achievement and course are entangled. All moves in course A come from high
achievers and all moves in course C from low achievers; only course B
contains both levels. Any difference between high and low achievers may
therefore partly reflect differences between courses. The last analytical
section returns to this.

## How do regulatory moves follow one another?

`context_tree()` reads the event log directly when the actor, time and state
columns are named. The tree is grown to a depth of three moves, and a
context needs at least ten occurrences to receive its own node.

```{r fit}
tree <- context_tree(group_regulation_long,
                     actor = "Actor", time = "Time", action = "Action",
                     max_depth = 3L, min_count = 10L)
tree
```

The tree is fitted on 2000 sequences (one per student) and 27533 moves. With
no history, the most likely next move is `consensus`, with probability 0.25;
this root distribution is the baseline that every longer context must
improve on. The unpruned tree holds 377 contexts, many of them deep
histories seen only a few dozen times.

`state_frequencies()` reports how often each move occurs.

```{r frequencies}
state_frequencies(tree)
```

`consensus` (24.7% of moves) and `plan` (24.1%) together account for almost
half of all regulation, followed by `discuss` (15.5%) and `emotion` (11.2%).
`synthesis` and `adapt` are rare, at 2.6% and 2.0%. This imbalance shapes
every later result: predicting `consensus` or `plan` is right a quarter of
the time without any history, so the informative contexts are those that
move the prediction away from these two defaults.

`common_pathways()` lists the most frequent histories and the move that most
often follows each.

```{r common}
common_pathways(tree, top = 8)
```

The first-order contexts already carry clear structure. After `consensus`
the most likely move is `plan` (0.40), and `plan` is most often followed by
another `plan` (0.37). `emotion` is followed by `cohesion` (0.33) and
`coregulate` by `discuss` (0.27). The `changes_prediction` column marks the
contexts whose most likely next move differs from that of the parent context.
The two most frequent second-order contexts, `consensus -> plan` and
`plan -> plan`, illustrate the opposite case: their next-move distributions
are almost identical to that of `plan` alone (`divergence` below 0.001), so
the extra move of history adds nothing to the prediction.

## How much history matters?

A grown tree keeps every context with enough occurrences, whether or not it
predicts better than its parent. `prune_tree()` removes a context when a
likelihood-ratio (G²) test does not show that the longer history changes the
next-move distribution relative to its one-move-shorter parent.

```{r prune}
pruned <- prune_tree(tree, criterion = "G2", alpha = 0.05)
pruned
```

Pruning reduces the tree from 377 to 23 nodes: the root, all nine
first-order contexts, eight second-order and five third-order contexts. The fit statistics of the two trees can be compared directly.

```{r fit-compare}
rbind(unpruned = model_fit(tree), pruned = model_fit(pruned))
```

The pruned tree uses 184 free parameters instead of 3016. Its in-sample
perplexity is slightly higher (5.43 against 5.21 equally likely next moves),
which is expected because the larger tree fits its own data more closely,
but its AIC (93509 against 96962) and BIC (95022 against 121763) are both
lower. Perplexity is the effective number of equally likely next moves; with
nine codes the uniform baseline is 9.

In-sample perplexity favors larger trees. `tune_tree()` gives a held-out
estimate: it splits the students into five folds, fits each configuration on
four and scores the fifth.

```{r tune}
tuned <- tune_tree(group_regulation_long,
                   actor = "Actor", time = "Time", action = "Action",
                   max_depth = 1L:3L, min_count = 10L,
                   prune = c(FALSE, TRUE), folds = 5L, seed = 1L)
summary(tuned)
as.data.frame(tuned)
```

The first-order model has the lowest held-out perplexity (5.46). The pruned
second-order tree is practically indistinguishable (5.47), and the pruned
third-order tree is close behind (5.49). The unpruned deeper trees generalize
worse: 5.53 at depth two and 5.88 at depth three, where the folds average 344
contexts. Collaborative regulation in these data therefore has short memory.
The current move carries almost all the predictive information, and the
longer contexts retained by pruning refine a small number of predictions
without improving overall held-out prediction.

`tree_dependence()` quantifies the contribution of each retained context in
bits: `entropy_drop` is the reduction in next-move uncertainty relative to
the parent context.

```{r dependence}
tree_dependence(pruned, sort_by = "entropy_drop", top = 8)
```

Among the first-order contexts, `adapt` removes the most uncertainty (0.75
bits): after an adaptation, the group almost always returns to `consensus`.
The largest drop overall belongs to `consensus -> cohesion -> plan` (1.40
bits), where the next move is `plan` with high probability, but this context
occurs only 12 times. `emotion -> emotion -> consensus` (58 occurrences)
lowers uncertainty by 0.60 bits relative to `emotion -> consensus`. The
bootstrap below asks which of these refinements are reproducible.

## Which pathways are reliable?

`bootstrap_pathways()` resamples students with replacement, refits the
pruned tree's contexts in each resample, and records two properties of each
pathway: whether its count stays within half to one and a half times the
observed count (`stable`), and whether its G² against the parent context
exceeds the chi-squared critical value in at least 80% of resamples
(`informative`).

```{r bootstrap}
boot <- bootstrap_pathways(pruned, iter = 199L, stat = "count", seed = 1L)
boot
```

Of the 23 pathways, 22 are stable, 14 are informative and 13 are both. The
summary table shows the bootstrap rates and the 95% interval of each
pathway's G² against its parent.

```{r bootstrap-summary}
summary(boot) |>
  subset(select = c(pathway, depth, count, stability_rate,
                    informative_rate, ci_G2_lo, ci_G2_hi, stable, informative))
```

All nine first-order contexts are both stable and informative. Four longer
pathways also meet both criteria: `discuss -> coregulate -> discuss`
(informative in 94.5% of resamples), `emotion -> emotion -> consensus`
(96.0%), `adapt -> discuss` (87.4%) and `cohesion -> cohesion` (83.4%). After
`adapt -> discuss`, the most likely next move is `adapt` again, whereas
`discuss` alone leads to `consensus`; an adaptation followed by discussion
tends to produce further adaptation. Several frequent second-order contexts,
such as `plan -> emotion` (831 occurrences) and `cohesion -> consensus`
(795), are stable but informative in fewer than 80% of resamples: they are
common, but their next-move distributions are not reproducibly different
from those of their parents. The striking `consensus -> cohesion -> plan`
context is stable but informative in only 63.3% of resamples, so its sharp
prediction should not be reported as a finding.

The forest plot draws the same intervals against the chi-squared critical
value.

```{r bootstrap-plot, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5.5}
plot(boot) + ggplot2::scale_x_log10()
```

Each bar is the bootstrap interval of a pathway's G², drawn on a logarithmic
axis so that the first-order contexts, whose G² runs into the thousands, do
not compress the longer pathways against the axis; the dashed line is the
critical value. The plot shows the 21 pathways with a stability rate of at
least 0.95. Pathways whose bars lie entirely to the right of the line
are reproducibly informative; those whose bars cross it are not.

## Do high and low achievers regulate differently?

Passing `group = "Achiever"` fits one tree per achievement level over a
shared alphabet. A depth of two keeps the number of compared contexts
manageable.

```{r groups}
grp <- context_tree(group_regulation_long,
                    actor = "Actor", time = "Time", action = "Action",
                    group = "Achiever", max_depth = 2L, min_count = 10L)
summary(grp)
```

Each level contributes 1000 students (13721 and 13812 moves), and the two
trees have similar size (74 and 77 contexts) and perplexity (5.26 and 5.28).
Overall predictability is therefore similar; the question is whether the
same histories lead to different moves.

`state_frequencies()` returns the move frequencies of each group.

```{r group-frequencies}
state_frequencies(grp)
```

High achievers make more `consensus` (26.6% against 22.8%), `emotion` (12.3%
against 10.1%) and `cohesion` moves (7.4% against 5.9%). Low achievers make
more `plan` (25.5% against 22.6%), `monitor` (6.1% against 4.9%) and `adapt`
moves (2.9% against 1.1%).

`compare_groups()` tests the difference with a permutation test. It shuffles
the achievement labels across sequences, refits the counts and compares two
omnibus statistics with their permutation distributions. The *behavioral*
statistic sums the Jensen-Shannon divergence between the groups' next-move
distributions over shared contexts, weighted by count; it asks whether the
same history leads to different moves. The *usage* statistic is a summed G²
homogeneity test of how often each group reaches each context. Per-context
p-values are adjusted with the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure.

```{r compare}
cmp <- compare_groups(grp, iter = 199L, seed = 1L)
summary(cmp)
```

Both omnibus p-values equal 0.005, the smallest value attainable with 199
permutations (1 / 200): no permutation produced a difference as large as the
observed one. After adjustment, 29 of the 80 contexts differ in their
next-move distributions and 45 in how often the groups reach them, and in 26
contexts the most likely next move differs between the groups.

The pathway table ranks contexts by behavioral divergence.

```{r compare-pathways}
as.data.frame(cmp, what = "pathways") |> head(10)
```

The largest divergences occur in rare contexts that involve `adapt` and
`synthesis`. After `synthesis -> discuss`, high achievers most often move to
`consensus` and low achievers to `synthesis`; after `adapt -> discuss`, high
achievers move to `consensus` and low achievers to `adapt`. These contexts
are seen 36 and 29 times, and their behavioral differences are not
significant after adjustment (`jsd_padj` 0.58), although low achievers reach
them more often (`usage_padj` 0.011). The individual top-ranked contexts are
too rare to carry the difference on their own; the significant behavioral
differences are spread over more frequent contexts further down the table.

`plot_difference()` maps where the groups differ. With `depth = 1` it shows
the first-order transitions; each cell is the Pearson residual of the high
achievers' next-move counts against the pooled expectation for that context,
and passing the comparison stars the contexts whose behavioral difference is
significant after adjustment.

```{r difference-plot, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5}
plot_difference(grp, depth = 1L, comparison = cmp)
```

Positive (red) cells mark next moves that high achievers make more often
than expected from the pooled data, negative (blue) cells moves they make
less often. Seven of the nine first-order contexts are starred. The largest
residuals are in the `discuss` row: after discussion, high achievers move to
`consensus` more often than expected (+8.2) and to `adapt` less often
(-7.9). High achievers also move from `consensus` to `discuss` (+6.0) and
from `plan` to `emotion` (+5.0) more often, and repeat `plan` less often
(-4.1). Low achievers thus adapt more after discussion and plan
repeatedly, whereas high achievers more often close a discussion with
consensus.

## Is the difference a course effect?

Course A contains only high achievers and course C only low achievers, so
the comparison above mixes achievement with course. Passing
`block = "Course"` stratifies the permutation: labels are shuffled only
within courses, which holds the course composition of each group fixed in
every permutation. Because courses A and C contain one achievement level
each, only the 700 students of course B are actually reshuffled.

```{r compare-stratified}
grp_course <- context_tree(group_regulation_long,
                           actor = "Actor", time = "Time", action = "Action",
                           group = "Achiever", block = "Course",
                           max_depth = 2L, min_count = 10L)
cmp_course <- compare_groups(grp_course, iter = 199L, seed = 1L)
summary(cmp_course)
```

Both omnibus p-values remain at 0.005. Under a null distribution that
preserves the confounding between course and achievement, the observed
difference is still larger than any permuted one, so it is not explained by
course composition alone. The number of individually significant contexts
falls, however, from 29 to 12 for behavior and from 45 to 10 for usage.
Many of the per-context differences in the unstratified test are therefore
attributable to differences between courses rather than to achievement
within a course.

## What the analysis shows

Collaborative regulation in these data has short memory. The current move
predicts the next one about as well as any longer history: the first-order
model has the lowest held-out perplexity, and pruning removes 354 of the 377
grown contexts. A few longer pathways reproducibly refine the prediction:
an adaptation followed by discussion tends to produce another adaptation,
and repeated emotional moves followed by consensus lead to planning. High
and low achievers differ both in the moves they make after the same history
and in how often they reach particular histories, and the difference
remains when the permutation holds course composition fixed.

The analysis has limits. The bundled data are an example dataset, so the
estimates illustrate the method rather than establish findings about
collaborative regulation. Achievement is constant within each collaboration
group, and students in the same group are not independent; the permutation
treats sequences as exchangeable, so its p-values are optimistic with
respect to group-level dependence. The stratified test holds course fixed,
but in courses A and C the two levels cannot be compared at all, so the
achievement contrast rests largely on course B. Finally, the 199 permutations
and resamples used here keep the article fast; a reported analysis should
use more.
